name: Vāsudeva (deity of early inscriptions)
subtype: deity attested in inscriptions and coins
summary: Vāsudeva is the deity named in the earliest Vaiṣṇava inscriptions of the 2nd–1st centuries BCE, such as the Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar, where he is called devadeva, “god of gods”. He was later identified with Kṛṣṇa and with Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa. The material record shows his worship centuries before the Purāṇic synthesis.
details:
In the material record Vāsudeva appears first as one of a pair with Saṅkarṣaṇa. On the Indian-standard drachms of the Greco-Bactrian king Agathocles found at Aï Khanoum (c. 190–180 BCE) he is usually identified as the figure holding a conch and a wheel. The Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar (late 2nd c. BCE) calls him devadeva and records a Garuḍa-standard set up by a Greek envoy who styles himself a bhāgavata. The Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions (2nd–1st c. BCE) and the Nāṇeghāṭ inscription of Nāganikā (1st c. BCE) invoke Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva together.

At Mathurā, the Mora well inscription (c. 15 CE) records images of the five Vṛṣṇi heroes, and the Vasu doorjamb inscription (early 1st c. CE) records a gateway and railing at a shrine of Bhagavat Vāsudeva, both from the time of the satrap Śoḍāsa. Grammatical literature mentions Vāsudeva earlier: Pāṇini 4.3.98 teaches the formation of a word for a devotee of Vāsudeva and Arjuna, and Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya refers to the slaying of Kaṃsa.

This record keeps Vāsudeva as a separate id from the epic character Kṛṣṇa (char:krishna). The identification of the two, and of Vāsudeva with Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa, is a historical synthesis attested in the epic and Purāṇic texts. It is recorded as an IDENTIFIED_WITH assertion (owned by the epic agent), not as a merge.

dates.label: c. 190–180 BCE (Agathocles coins; identification argued)
dates.basis: coin issue dated by the reign of Agathocles; the deity identification is scholarly

dates.label: late 2nd century BCE (Heliodorus pillar)
dates.basis: regnal synchronism with the Indo-Greek king Antialkidas; Brāhmī palaeography

limits: Establishes that Vāsudeva was worshipped by the late 2nd century BCE in central and western India, and by Greek envoys. It does not establish the historicity of the Kṛṣṇa of the epic or Purāṇas, nor the date at which Vāsudeva was identified with Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra or with Viṣṇu.
openQuestions: When was Vāsudeva first explicitly identified with Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa in a dated inscription?
How did the Vṛṣṇi-hero cult at Mathurā relate to the bhāgavata devotion recorded at Besnagar and Nagari?

name: Saṅkarṣaṇa (deity of early inscriptions)
subtype: deity attested in inscriptions and coins
summary: Saṅkarṣaṇa is the deity invoked together with Vāsudeva in inscriptions of the 2nd–1st centuries BCE, and is usually named first. He is identified with Balarāma, Kṛṣṇa's elder brother, and later became the first emanation (vyūha) of Vāsudeva in Pāñcarātra theology.
details:
Saṅkarṣaṇa is invoked with Vāsudeva in the compound “Saṃkarṣaṇa-Vāsudeva” in the Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions of king Sarvatāta, who had a stone enclosure built for their worship. He appears again in the opening invocation of the Nāṇeghāṭ inscription of the Sātavāhana queen Nāganikā. On the Agathocles drachms from Aï Khanoum (c. 190–180 BCE), the figure holding a plough and a pestle or club is identified as Saṅkarṣaṇa-Balarāma. Scholars take him to be one of the five Vṛṣṇi heroes of the Mora well inscription. That identification rests on the later Purāṇic list of the five, not on the inscription itself.

The graph keeps the deity of the inscriptions apart from the epic character Balarāma (char:balarama). The two are joined by an IDENTIFIED_WITH assertion qualified by tradition.
limits: The inscriptions show a cult of Saṅkarṣaṇa paired with Vāsudeva before the Common Era. They do not show the narrative of Balarāma as told in the Harivaṃśa or the Purāṇas, nor that the pair's legends already existed in their later form.

name: Heliodorus pillar inscription, Besnagar
summary: Two Brāhmī inscriptions in Prakrit on a stone pillar at Besnagar (ancient Vidiśā) record that Heliodorus of Taxila set up a Garuḍa-standard (garuḍadhvaja) for Vāsudeva, “god of gods”. Heliodorus, son of Dion, calls himself a bhāgavata and was a Greek envoy of the Indo-Greek king Antialkidas to king Kāsīputra Bhāgabhadra. It is among the earliest dated pieces of evidence for Vāsudeva devotion.
details:
The main inscription (A) says that this Garuḍa-standard of Vāsudeva, the god of gods, was made by Heliodorus. He is described as a bhāgavata, the son of Dion, a man of Taxila, and a Greek ambassador who came from the great king Antialkidas to king Kāsīputra Bhāgabhadra, the Saviour, in his fourteenth regnal year. The second, shorter inscription (B) names three immortal steps (amuta-pādāni) which, when practised, lead to heaven: self-restraint (dama), generosity (cāga) and attentiveness (apramāda).

Alexander Cunningham noticed the pillar during his tours of the 1870s. Wikipedia gives both 1874–75 and 1877, so the year is inconsistent in the sources checked. The inscriptions were found only in 1909, after a team led by H. H. Lake cleaned away the red paint; John Marshall reported them. D. R. Bhandarkar excavated around the pillar in 1913–15, and M. D. Khare's excavation of 1963–65 found the foundations of an elliptical temple next to it.

Dating: the record dates itself only to Bhāgabhadra's 14th regnal year, so its absolute date depends on the reign of Antialkidas. Bopearachchi dates that reign c. 115–95 BCE and R. C. Senior c. 130–120 BCE. The often-quoted single year “113 BCE” is a convention and is not stated in the inscription. Whether Bhāgabhadra was a Śuṅga king or a local ruler is also disputed.

It does not identify Vāsudeva with the epic Kṛṣṇa or with Viṣṇu, and it does not show that any epic event took place. The parallel between inscription B and a Mahābhārata verse is an interpretation (claim:heliodorus-mbh-parallel).
openQuestions: Which year (1874–75 or 1877) did Cunningham first record the pillar?
Was Bhāgabhadra a Śuṅga king (the Purāṇic Bhāgavata?) or a local ruler of Vidiśā?

name: Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions
summary: Three fragmentary Sanskrit inscriptions in Brāhmī script from Ghosuṇḍī and Hāthībāḍā near Nagari (ancient Madhyamikā), Rajasthan, dated to the 2nd–1st century BCE. They record that king Sarvatāta of the Gājāyana lineage, a devotee of Bhagavat and performer of an aśvamedha, built a stone enclosure for the worship of Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva, called Nārāyaṇa-vāṭikā. They are among the earliest Sanskrit (as opposed to Prakrit) inscriptions.
details:
Three incomplete copies (fragments A, B, C) are known. One was in an ancient well at Ghosuṇḍī, one in a boundary wall between Ghosuṇḍī and Bassi, and one in the inner wall of the Hāthībāḍā enclosure near Nagari. The legible words include Gājāyana, Pārāśarīputra, Sarvatāta, aśvamedha-yājin, Saṃkarṣaṇa-Vāsudeva, pūjāśilā-prākāra (stone enclosure for worship) and Nārāyaṇa-vāṭikā.

D. R. Bhandarkar's edition (Epigraphia Indica 22) reads the record as the building of the enclosure called Nārāyaṇa-vāṭikā for Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva. Harry Falk notes that the king names neither his father nor the title rāja. The record matters because it links the Vṛṣṇi pair with the name Nārāyaṇa, and because a royal patron combines Vedic royal ritual (the aśvamedha) with bhāgavata devotion.

limits: Shows royal patronage of a joint cult of Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva in Rajasthan before the Common Era, and an early link with the name Nārāyaṇa. It says nothing about the narrative life of Kṛṣṇa or Balarāma, and the fragmentary text leaves the exact form of the shrine uncertain.
openQuestions: Is 'Nārāyaṇa-vāṭikā' the name of the enclosure or evidence that Nārāyaṇa was already identified with the pair?

name: Nāṇeghāṭ inscription of Nāganikā
summary: A long Brāhmī cave inscription at the Nāṇeghāṭ pass (Maharashtra), commissioned by the Sātavāhana queen Nāganikā (Nāyanikā). It opens by invoking Dharma, Indra, Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva, the lunar line and the four Lokapālas (Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, Vāsava), and lists Vedic sacrifices, including two horse sacrifices, with the fees paid for them. Most scholars date it to the 1st century BCE.
details:
The inscription is cut on the walls of a rock-cut rest-house at the head of a trade route over the Western Ghats. It is attributed to queen Nāganikā (Nāyanikā), probably the widow of Sātakarṇi, acting as queen mother for her son. It records Vedic rites such as the agnyādheya, rājasūya, two aśvamedhas, the gavāmayana and various soma rituals, together with the cattle, coins and other fees given for them.

Documentation: William Sykes made an eye-copy in 1828 and published it in 1833/1837; Bhagvanlal Indraji gave a partial translation in 1878; Georg Bühler published the first complete edition in 1883. Dating views: D. C. Sircar puts it in the second half of the 1st century BCE, and Upinder Singh in the 1st century BCE. Some scholars prefer the 2nd century BCE, and Alcock places it after Kaṇha's Nasik inscription on palaeographic grounds.

location.label: Naneghat pass, Pune district, Maharashtra, India (in situ)

name: Mora well inscription (Mathurā)
summary: A fragmentary Sanskrit inscription on a stone slab from the Mora well near Mathurā, from the time of the Mahākṣatrapa Śoḍāsa, son of Rājuvula (c. 15 CE). It records the installation of images (pratimā) of the five Vṛṣṇi heroes (pañcavīra), called bhagavat, in a stone shrine linked to a woman named Toṣā. It is the earliest epigraphic reference to cult images of the Vṛṣṇi heroes.
details:
Line 2 of the slab refers to the images (pratimā[ḥ]) of the holy five heroes (paṃcavīrāṇāṃ) of the Vṛṣṇis (vṛṣṇīnā[ṃ]), with the epithet bhagavatāṃ. The inscription names the Great Satrap Rājuvula. It is generally taken to date from the rule of his son Śoḍāsa, and Quintanilla gives c. 15 CE. The slab and a male torso, probably one of the five heroes, are in the Government Museum, Mathurā; the slab is identified as GMM Q.1.

The inscription does not name the five heroes. Scholars identify them as Saṅkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, Sāmba and Aniruddha by comparison with a later Purāṇic list (Vāyu Purāṇa). That identification is an argument, not a reading. The Mora mound was excavated in 1911–12.

dates.label: c. 15 CE (time of Śoḍāsa)
dates.basis: names Mahākṣatrapa Rājuvula; satrapal chronology of Mathurā; palaeography

name: Torso of a Vṛṣṇi hero from Mora
summary: A stone male torso of c. 15 CE found at Mora near Mathurā together with the Mora well inscription and a carved doorjamb. It is now in the Government Museum, Mathurā, and is probably one of the five Vṛṣṇi heroes whose images the inscription records. It is among the earliest surviving cult images associated with the Vāsudeva–Saṅkarṣaṇa group.
details: Wikipedia's caption describes it as a 'torso probably of one of the five Vrishni heroes, Mora, circa 15 CE, Mathura Museum'. The mound also produced two male torsos and the lower half of a female torso inscribed with the names Kaniṣka and Toṣā; their present location is not stated. Which hero the torso represents cannot be determined.

dates.label: c. 15 CE
dates.basis: association with the dated Mora well inscription; style

location.label: Findspot: Mora, near Mathura, Uttar Pradesh, India

attributes.findspot: Mora mound/well, near Mathurā

limits: Shows that the Vṛṣṇi heroes were worshipped as life-size anthropomorphic images in the early 1st century CE. The identity of the individual hero is unknown, and the torso is not evidence for the narratives about them.

name: Vasu doorjamb inscription (Mathurā)
summary: A twelve-line Sanskrit inscription in Brāhmī on the back of a red sandstone doorjamb found in an old well at Mathurā. It dates from the time of the Mahākṣatrapa Śoḍāsa (early 1st century CE) and records that a donor named Vasu set up a gateway (toraṇa) and railing (vedikā) at the great shrine of Bhagavat Vāsudeva. It is held in the Government Museum, Mathurā (GMM 13.367).
details:
The first five lines are too damaged to read. The last seven mention a toraṇa, a vedikā and a shrine (mahāsthāna) of Bhagavat Vāsudeva established in Śoḍāsa's time; the name Vāsudeva survives as “-devaḥ” in line 10. Readings differ. Chanda (1920) read catuḥśāla, a quadrangle; N. P. Chakravarti (Epigraphia Indica 24, 1942) thought that unlikely and suggested devakula or śaila; Quintanilla (2007) translates “a stone toraṇa and railing were erected by Vasu at the great temple of Vāsudeva”.

Dating: Salomon places the inscription in Śoḍāsa's time, early 1st century CE, and Quintanilla c. 15 CE. Joanna Williams suggested the carving of the jamb might be later (3rd century CE); Quintanilla argues that carving and inscription are both 1st century.

dates.label: 3rd century CE (carving of the jamb)
dates.view: J. Williams (carving later than the text)

attributes.findspot: an old well at Mathurā (red sandstone doorjamb)
attributes.reading: legible portion mentions toraṇa, vedikā and the shrine of bhagavat Vāsudeva in the time of Śoḍāsa; “-devaḥ” in line 10 (per Wikipedia)

limits: Establishes a shrine of Bhagavat Vāsudeva at Mathurā with stone gateway and railing in the early 1st century CE. It is not evidence for the Kṛṣṇa-janmabhūmi tradition at any specific modern site, nor for the historicity of Kṛṣṇa's birth at Mathurā.

name: Coins of Agathocles with Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva
summary: Six Indian-standard silver drachms of the Greco-Bactrian king Agathocles (c. 190–180 BCE), found in 1970 at Aï Khanoum (Afghanistan), each show two male deities. One holds a plough and a pestle or club, the other a conch and a wheel. They are usually identified as Saṅkarṣaṇa-Balarāma and Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa, and are often called the earliest unambiguous images of the Vṛṣṇi heroes.
details:
On 3 October 1970 the French archaeological mission (DAFA) found a hoard in a small room of the palace administrative quarter at Aï Khanoum. It held 677 punch-marked coins and six silver drachms in the name of Agathocles. The drachms carry the deity with plough and pestle or club on the Greek-legend side and the deity with conch and wheel on the Brāhmī side; the Brāhmī legend is given as Rājane Agathukleyesa, “of king Agathocles”.

Evidence class: the coins themselves are class 4. That they show Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva is a scholarly identification (class 5), based on the attributes and on the pairing in later Indian inscriptions. The coins show that the iconography of the pair already existed far from Mathurā in the early 2nd century BCE. Aï Khanoum was later looted, and the present whereabouts of the six drachms could not be verified.

name: Megasthenes’ “Herakles” of the Sourasenoi as Kṛṣṇa
subtype: identification of a deity in a Greek ethnography
summary: Megasthenes (c. 300 BCE), as excerpted by Arrian, Diodorus and Strabo, reported that an Indian people called the Sourasenoi especially honoured “Herakles”. They had two great cities, Methora and Kleisobora, and the navigable river Iobares ran through their land. Many scholars identify this Herakles with (Hari-)Kṛṣṇa, the Sourasenoi with the Śūrasenas, Methora with Mathurā and the Iobares with the Yamunā. Others propose Indra, Śiva or Balarāma, or doubt that the Greek label maps onto a single Indian deity.
details:
The case for: the geography fits closely (Śūrasena country, Mathurā, the Yamunā). Grammatical and epigraphic evidence shows Vāsudeva devotion by the 2nd century BCE (Pāṇini 4.3.98; Heliodorus pillar; Agathocles coins). Edwin Bryant writes that there is little doubt the Sourasenoi are the Śūrasenas.

The case against, or for caution: Greek authors routinely mapped foreign gods onto Herakles or Dionysos by analogy. Megasthenes' Herakles is “earth-born”, is credited with founding cities and with a daughter, Pandaia, and carries Herakles' club and lion-skin. These are Greek traits, not specifically Kṛṣṇa's. Dahlquist (1962) argued for Indra. Puskás (cited on Wikipedia) notes there is no independent evidence of Kṛṣṇa worship as early as the 4th century BCE. The fragments survive only as later excerpts.
limits: Even if correct, the identification shows only that a Herakles-like deity was honoured in the Mathurā region c. 300 BCE as perceived by a Greek observer. It does not establish the content of Kṛṣṇa narratives at that date or the historicity of Kṛṣṇa.
openQuestions: Can the Kleisobora of the fragments be securely located?
Does 'Herakles' render Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Saṅkarṣaṇa-Balarāma, or a generic heroic god?

name: Chāndogya’s Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra as the epic Kṛṣṇa
summary: The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (CU 3.17.6) names a Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra, “son of Devakī”, as a pupil of Ghora Āṅgirasa who learns a teaching that allegorises the sacrifice. Some scholars take him to be the epic and Purāṇic Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī, which would be the earliest textual reference to Kṛṣṇa. Others regard the shared name and matronymic as a coincidence, or the verse as an unrelated figure.
details:
For the identification: the name together with the matronymic Devakīputra is distinctive. Raychaudhuri (1920) and others built early Vaiṣṇava history on it, and some note parallels between Ghora's teaching and ideas in the Bhagavad Gītā. Max Müller allowed that the verse might be a source of later Kṛṣṇa lore. Archer argues the shared name in one verse cannot easily be dismissed.

Against: the Upaniṣadic passage gives no Vṛṣṇi, Yādava or epic context, and the name Kṛṣṇa was not rare. The later Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtras, which cite other Upaniṣads, never use this verse (noted on Wikipedia). Bryant and Ekstrand allow that the Chāndogya figure may be a different person. The vedic agent's char:krishna-devakiputra is therefore kept apart from char:krishna.

dates.label: c. 7th–6th century BCE (Chāndogya, as commonly dated)
dates.basis: scholarly dating of the early prose Upaniṣads

limits: A single verse naming a pupil cannot by itself establish that the epic Kṛṣṇa tradition existed in the Upaniṣadic period; nor can the absence of context disprove it.
openQuestions: Is there any datable intermediate source linking Devakīputra with the Vṛṣṇis before the Mahābhārata?

name: Heliodorus inscription B echoes a Mahābhārata verse
subtype: textual parallel claimed for an inscription
summary: Inscription B on the Heliodorus pillar lists three immortal steps: self-restraint, generosity and attentiveness (dama, cāga, apramāda). Since Raychaudhuri, scholars have compared this triad with a verse in the Mahābhārata's Strīparvan (MBh book 11). Some treat it as evidence that the epic, or its ethical verse tradition, was known in Vidiśā in the late 2nd century BCE.
details: Wikipedia, citing Irwin and Raychaudhuri, says inscription B “recites a verse” from the Mahābhārata. The Krishna article gives the locator as Mahābhārata 11.7. This record does not supply a Critical-Edition verse number because none was verified. A shared triad of virtues may come from a common pool of gnomic verse rather than from the epic itself, so the parallel does not date the Mahābhārata.

dates.label: late 2nd century BCE (date of the inscription)

limits: At most this shows the triad dama–tyāga–apramāda circulated by the late 2nd century BCE. It does not show that the Mahābhārata existed in written or epic form at that time.
openQuestions: Which Critical Edition verse (MBh 11.7.x) is the closest parallel, and is the triad attested elsewhere (e.g. in Buddhist or Jain gnomic verse)?

name: “Paśupati” seal, Mohenjo-daro
summary: A steatite stamp seal (c. 3.56 × 3.53 cm) excavated at Mohenjo-daro in 1928–29. It shows a horned, seated figure, possibly three-faced, in a yoga-like posture, surrounded by an elephant, a tiger, a water buffalo and a rhinoceros, with two deer or ibexes below and seven Indus signs above. John Marshall called it a “proto-Śiva” as Paśupati, lord of animals. The identification has been widely disputed since the 1960s. The seal is now in the National Museum, New Delhi.
details:
Findspot: Block 1, southern portion of the DK-G area of Mohenjo-daro, at a depth of 3.9 m, during the 1928–29 season of the Archaeological Survey of India. Ernest Mackay, who directed the excavations, numbered it 420 in his report Further Excavations at Mohenjo-daro (1938). He assigned it to his Intermediate I period, now roughly 2350–2000 BCE. At Partition in 1947 it was allocated to India and is held in the National Museum, New Delhi.

The iconography is described neutrally as a horned headdress, bangles, a seated posture with heels together, surrounding animals, and an undeciphered inscription. Because the Indus script is not read, any identification of the figure is an interpretation (see claim:proto-shiva).

attributes.findspot: Mohenjo-daro, DK-G area, Block 1, depth 3.9 m (1928–29)

attributes.discovered: 1928–29 season, ASI (excavation directed by E. J. H. Mackay)

limits: Establishes that a horned, seated figure among animals was a motif of Mature Harappan glyptic art. Without a deciphered script it cannot establish the figure's name or role, or any continuity with the later Śiva of Vedic, epic or Purāṇic religion.
openQuestions: What is the National Museum's accession number for the seal?
Do the other Mohenjo-daro seated-figure seals (e.g. nos. 222, 235) share the same iconography?

name: The “proto-Śiva” interpretation of the Paśupati seal
subtype: identification of a prehistoric image with a later deity
summary: John Marshall (1928–29; Mohenjo-daro and the Indus Civilization, 1931) proposed that the seated horned figure on the Mohenjo-daro seal 420 is a prototype of Śiva as Paśupati (lord of animals) and Mahāyogin. His view was widely accepted for about two generations. Since the 1960s it has been contested on iconographic, methodological and chronological grounds. There is no scholarly consensus.
details:
Marshall's arguments: (1) the figure is three-faced, possibly with a fourth face behind, like later multi-faced Śiva; (2) the horned headdress resembles a trident; (3) the posture is yogic (Śiva as Mahāyogin); (4) the surrounding animals suggest Paśupati; (5) in 1931 he added a possible ithyphallic feature and the deer below the seat.

Critiques: Sullivan (1964) argued for a female figure, reading the “phallus” as the end of a girdle. Doris Srinivasan (1975–76; 1997) argued that the side “faces” are bovine ears and the figure a buffalo-man, not a proto-Śiva. Hiltebeitel (1978) read the horns as a buffalo's and linked the figure to Mahiṣa and to the goddess's vāhanas. Parpola compared Proto-Elamite seated bulls and linked the figure to an aquatic deity; Fairservis and Krishna Rao proposed other identifications (the latter Indra). Doniger and Samuel urge caution, and Samuel notes the interpretations “certainly cannot all be right”. A methodological objection is that the Indus script is undeciphered and that some 1,500 years separate the seal from the earliest clear Śaiva texts and images.
limits: The claim cannot at present be verified or falsified. Even if the figure were a deity of animals, that would not establish continuity of name, cult or theology with historical Śaivism.
openQuestions: Would a decipherment of the Indus script, or a bilingual, settle the figure's identity?

name: Gudimallam liṅga
summary: A stone liṅga about 1.5 m high in the Paraśurāmeśvara temple at Gudimallam, near Tirupati (Andhra Pradesh). It carries a standing two-armed figure in high relief, holding a ram or antelope and a water pot, with an axe on the shoulder, standing on a crouching dwarf or yakṣa. It is widely regarded as one of the earliest surviving liṅgas with a figural Śiva. Dates proposed range from the 3rd century BCE to the 3rd–4th century CE.
details:
The liṅga is carved from hard, dark brown local stone, with a seven-faceted shaft about a foot in diameter. It is still in worship and stands in a square stone enclosure with a modern golden frame. The temple building itself is later (Cōḻa and Vijayanagara periods) and has been protected by the ASI since 1954.

In 1973–74 the ASI under I. K. Sarma (Karthikeya Sharma) excavated around it. They found that the liṅga originally had a pedestal, along with Sātavāhana-period sherds, Black-and-Red Ware attributed to the 2nd–3rd century CE, and large bricks. Dating views: Harle and Blurton put it in the 2nd–1st century BCE, and Elgood at the end of the BCE period into the 1st century CE. P. Arundhati compares it with Bharhut, Karle and Nāṇeghāṭ sculpture and proposes an early Sātavāhana date. Doniger suggests the 3rd century BCE. Other authors propose the 2nd or 3rd–4th century CE.

name: The Gudimallam liṅga dates to the 2nd–1st century BCE
summary: Several art historians (e.g. Harle) date the Gudimallam liṅga to the 2nd–1st century BCE on stylistic grounds. If correct, it is the earliest surviving figural liṅga in worship. Other scholars prefer dates in the early centuries CE, partly because of finds from the 1973–74 excavation.
limits: Whatever its date, the liṅga does not by itself date the textual liṅga myths (e.g. Liṅgodbhava) or Śaiva theology.
openQuestions: Could scientific dating (e.g. of associated organic material) refine the stylistic dates?

name: Oesho (OHÞO), deity of Kuṣāṇa coins
summary: Oesho (Bactrian ΟΗϷΟ) is the name of a deity on Kuṣāṇa coins from Kaniṣka I onward. On some issues he is shown with a bull, a trident and, from Huviṣka, several heads and four arms. Many numismatists identify him with Śiva. Others, notably Katsumi Tanabe and Helmut Humbach, read the name as the Iranian wind god Vāyu (Wēš), whose image took on Śaiva features.
details: The Bactrian legend OHÞO appears on gold and copper coins of Kaniṣka I, Huviṣka and Vāsudeva I, and later on coins of the later Kuṣāṇas. The figure's attributes include the trident, the vajra, a water pot, the bull, and on some coins multiple heads and arms. The graph does not merge Oesho with Śiva. Two IDENTIFIED_WITH assertions record the competing readings (deity:shiva; deity:vayu), and claim:oesho-shiva-identity holds the debate.
limits: The coins establish that a deity named Oesho with Śaiva-like attributes was part of the Kuṣāṇa royal pantheon. They do not establish whether Kuṣāṇa viewers understood him as Śiva, as Vāyu, or as both.

name: Oesho on Kuṣāṇa coins is Śiva
summary: The traditional numismatic view holds that the Kuṣāṇa coin deity Oesho is Śiva, as his trident, bull and multiple heads and arms suggest. The alternative view holds that Oesho is the Bactrian form of the Iranian wind god Vāyu (Wēš). On this view the Śaiva iconography was borrowed and full syncretism with Śiva came later, as seen in Sogdian Weshparkar.
details:
For: the iconography of trident, bull, ithyphallic figure on some Wima Kadphises coppers and multi-headed figures on Huviṣka's issues. Wima Kadphises' Kharoṣṭhī legend includes mahiśvarasa, read by many as “of the devotee of Maheśvara (Śiva)”, though others read it as a royal epithet. A Kharoṣṭhī inscription from Māṭ near Mathurā is reported to commemorate Wima as devoted to, and receiving his kingdom from, Śiva.

Against: the name ΟΗϷΟ is best explained as Bactrian for Vāyu (Avestan vaiiu), and the Rabatak inscription lists Iranian deities. Tanabe (1997) argues the coin deity is Vāyu and that Śaiva syncretism came later through Sogdian art. Humbach reads Weshparkar as Vayuš uparō kairyō.
limits: Resolving the identification would clarify Kuṣāṇa religious policy, but neither reading establishes the content of contemporary Śaiva texts.

name: Gold coins of Wima Kadphises with a deity and bull
subtype: coin type (gold double stater, stater, quarter stater; copper)
summary: Gold and copper coins of the Kuṣāṇa king Wima (Vima) Kadphises show on the reverse a deity holding a long trident, sometimes with a bull and on some coppers ithyphallic, together with the triratna or nandipada symbol. The Kharoṣṭhī legend calls the king mahiśvara, read by many as “devotee of Maheśvara”. The deity is usually identified with Śiva. Wima was also the first Kuṣāṇa ruler to issue gold coins.
details:
Obverse: the king, with Greek legend ΒΑΣΙΛΕΥΣ ΟΟΗΜΟ ΚΑΔΦΙΣΗΣ. Reverse: a deity with a long trident, sometimes with a bull. The Kharoṣṭhī legend as given on Wikipedia reads MAHARAJASA RAJADIRAJASA SARVALOGA ISVARASA MAHISVARASA VIMA KATHPHISASA TRADARA. The gold standard was about 8 g, in double staters, staters and quarter staters.

The core registry calls this the 'Oesho coin'. On Wima's own coins the deity is not labelled OHÞO; that label appears from Kaniṣka I onward (see art:kushan-oesho-coins). This entity is a coin type, not one specimen. Cleveland Museum of Art 1999.225 is a Wima gold coin with a Herakles reverse, a different type.

dates.label: c. 50–78 CE (older chronology)
dates.basis: pre-Rabatak chronology used in some museum records

attributes.reading: Kharoṣṭhī legend (per Wikipedia): MAHARAJASA RAJADIRAJASA SARVALOGA ISVARASA MAHISVARASA VIMA KATHPHISASA TRADARA

sources.locator: 1999.225 (Wima Kadphises gold coin, Hercules reverse — a different type)

limits: Establishes Śaiva-style iconography and probably Śaiva devotion in Kuṣāṇa royal imagery in the late 1st or early 2nd century CE. It does not show which Śaiva texts or sects existed, and the epithet mahiśvara is open to more than one reading.

name: Kuṣāṇa coins naming OHÞO (Oesho)
summary: Gold and copper coin types of Kaniṣka I, Huviṣka and Vāsudeva I bear the Bactrian legend ΟΗϷΟ (Oesho) beside a deity with a trident, vajra, water pot and sometimes a bull. Under Huviṣka the deity has three heads and four arms. The type is central to the debate over whether Oesho is Śiva or the Iranian Vāyu.
details: Captions on Wikipedia's Oesho article show Oesho with bull and trident on coins of Vāsudeva I, holding vajra and trident on coins of Huviṣka, and with a worshipper on a 3rd-century Bactrian issue. Kaniṣka's coins place Oesho in a mixed pantheon with Mao (moon), Miiro (sun), Nana, Oado (wind) and the Buddha. That makes a simple 'Hindu' reading of the series misleading.

dates.label: c. 127–230 CE (Kaniṣka I to Vāsudeva I)

limits: The series shows a named deity with Śaiva-like attributes in the Kuṣāṇa royal pantheon. The name points to an Iranian origin, so it cannot alone establish Śiva worship by the Kuṣāṇa court.

name: Varāha relief, Udayagiri Cave 5
summary: A monumental rock-cut relief in the shallow niche called Cave 5 at Udayagiri near Vidiśā. It shows Viṣṇu as the boar-headed Varāha lifting the Earth goddess, who clings to his tusk, out of the cosmic ocean, watched by rows of gods and sages. It dates from the reign of the Gupta king Candragupta II (c. 401–412 CE) and is among the most studied reliefs of the Gupta period.
details:
Varāha stands in a heroic posture with the goddess Earth (Bhūdevī or Pṛthvī) at his tusk. The surrounding registers include Brahmā, Śiva, the Ādityas, Agni, Vāyu, the Vasus and Rudras, ṛṣis, a nāga king, and the sages Nārada and Tumburu. The Udayagiri article identifies a kneeling figure below as probably Candragupta II, with his minister Vīrasena.

Dating: no inscription is cut on the panel. Its date rests on the dated Gupta inscriptions of the same hill, Cave 6 (Gupta year 82 = 401/402 CE) and Cave 8 (Vīrasena). Heinrich von Stietencron proposed 410–412 CE and linked the panel to Candragupta's assumption of the title Vikramāditya. Michael Willis (2009) reads the hill as a royal ritual landscape tied to the solstice.

dates.label: c. 401–415 CE (reign of Candragupta II)
dates.basis: association with Cave 6 inscription of Gupta year 82 and the Cave 8 inscription of Vīrasena

name: Udayagiri Cave 6 inscription of the time of Candragupta II (year 82)
aliases: Udayagiri Cave Inscription of Chandragupta II, Year 82
summary: A short Sanskrit inscription at the entrance of Udayagiri Cave 6, dated year 82 (Gupta era, 401/402 CE), on the 11th day of the bright half of Āṣāḍha. It records the pious gift (deyadharma) of a Sanakānīka mahārāja, son of Viṣṇudāsa and grandson of Chagalaga, who calls himself a devotee of the feet of the paramabhaṭṭāraka mahārājādhirāja Candragupta. It is the earliest dated record of Candragupta II.
details: The edition on Dharmalekha (from the Siddham project) gives the date as “saṁvatsare 80 2” in Āṣāḍha, śukla 11, and the key word deyadharmmaḥ, “pious gift”. The donor's personal name or domain after “mahārāja” is lost. Fleet suggested “ḍha” and Sircar “Soḍhala”, but both are guesses. The first critical edition is Fleet 1888 (CII III, item 3).

location.label: Udayagiri hills, near Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh, India (in situ)

attributes.findspot: Udayagiri Cave 6
attributes.reading: “saṁvatsare 80 2 …” (year 82) … “deyadharmmaḥ” … Sanakānika mahārāja, son of mahārāja Viṣṇudāsa, grandson of mahārāja Chagalaga … pādānuddhyāta of Candragupta (per Dharmalekha)

limits: Dates Gupta-period activity at Udayagiri to 401/402 CE and shows a feudatory acknowledging Candragupta II. It records a gift but does not name the deity of Cave 6, and it does not date every sculpture on the hill.

name: Udayagiri Cave 8 inscription of Vīrasena
summary: A five-line Sanskrit verse inscription in Udayagiri Cave 8 (the Tawa cave). It records that Vīrasena of the Kautsa gotra, surnamed Śāba, a minister of Candragupta II, made the cave as a temple of Śambhu (Śiva) when he came to the place with the king. It is undated but falls within Candragupta II's reign.
details: The inscription shows Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava foundations side by side on a hill patronised by the Gupta court. The Varāha relief is Vaiṣṇava, and this record says the cave was made out of devotion to Śambhu.

location.label: Udayagiri hills, near Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh, India (in situ)

attributes.findspot: Udayagiri Cave 8 (Tawa cave)

limits: Establishes royal-ministerial Śaiva patronage in Candragupta II's reign. It does not describe Śaiva doctrine or ritual.

name: Iron pillar inscription of Candra (Delhi)
summary: A Sanskrit verse inscription on the wrought-iron pillar now in the Qutb complex, Mehrauli, Delhi. It records that a king named Candra, a devotee of Viṣṇu, set up a standard (dhvaja) of Viṣṇu on a hill called Viṣṇupada. By script and style it dates to the late 4th or early 5th century CE, and Candra is generally identified with Candragupta II.
details: The pillar is 7.21 m high, forge-welded wrought iron weighing over six tonnes. Its resistance to corrosion is attributed to a high phosphorus content. Where it first stood is disputed. Fleet (1898) suggested Mathurā. Dass and Balasubramaniam (2004), followed by Michael Willis, proposed Udayagiri. F. B. Flood (2009) argued it was brought from Vidiśā by Iltutmish. A later short inscription of Samvat 1109 is linked with the Tomara king Anaṅgapāla, and its reading is contested.

dates.label: late 4th – early 5th century CE
dates.basis: palaeography; poetic style; identification of Candra with Candragupta II

location.label: Qutb complex, Mehrauli, Delhi, India (present location; not original)

attributes.repository: in situ at Qutb complex (moved from an original site)

limits: Shows royal Vaiṣṇava devotion and the erection of a Viṣṇu-dhvaja c. 400 CE. It does not say where Viṣṇupada was, and the identification of Candra is argued, not stated.
openQuestions: Was the pillar's original site Udayagiri, Mathurā or elsewhere?

name: Colossal Varāha of Eran
summary: A free-standing red sandstone image of Varāha in full boar form, about 4.2 m long and 3.4 m high, standing in the open at Eran (ancient Airikiṇa). Small figures of gods and sages cover its body and the Earth goddess hangs from its tusk. An eight-line Sanskrit inscription on its chest is dated in the first regnal year of the Hūṇa king Toramāṇa. It records that Dhanyaviṣṇu, younger brother of the late Mātṛviṣṇu, had a stone temple built for Nārāyaṇa in the form of a boar.
details: The image stands among the ruins of a Gupta-period temple group at Eran, a site whose inscriptions run from Samudragupta to the Goparāja memorial pillar of 510 CE. Cunningham reported the site in ASI Reports vol. X (1880). The Wikipedia article on the inscription gives its date as after 510 and before 513 CE, following R. K. Mookerji. The Toramana article also gives the bound 'after 484/85 CE', which leaves a wider range open.

name: Eran boar inscription of Toramāṇa
summary: An eight-line Sanskrit inscription in Brāhmī on the chest of the colossal Varāha at Eran, dated the 10th day of Phālguna in the first year of the reign of the mahārājādhirāja Toramāṇa. It records that Dhanyaviṣṇu, younger brother of the deceased mahārāja Mātṛviṣṇu, built a stone temple of the boar-formed Nārāyaṇa at Airikiṇa (Eran).
details: The first three lines are in verse and the rest in prose. Fleet's and Hall's translations differ in wording but agree on the content. The inscription is a key document for the Hūṇa (Alchon) advance into central India. The Toramana article quotes its opening: “In year one of the reign of the King of Kings Sri-Toramana …”.

name: Eran pillar inscription of the time of Budhagupta (Gupta year 165)
summary: A Sanskrit inscription on a monolithic pillar at Eran topped by a double Garuḍa with a wheel behind. It is dated Gupta year 165 (484/485 CE) in the reign of Budhagupta and records the erection of the pillar as a standard in honour of Janārdana (Viṣṇu).
details: According to Fleet's edition the pillar was raised by the brothers Mātṛviṣṇu and Dhanyaviṣṇu, the same family as the boar inscription. The Wikipedia article checked does not name them, so this detail is marked from recall. Together, the two records show one local family moving from Gupta to Hūṇa suzerainty within a generation.

name: Gajendramokṣa panel, Daśāvatāra temple, Deogarh
summary: A relief niche (about 3.25 × 5 ft) on the north wall of the Gupta-period Daśāvatāra temple at Deogarh. It shows the elephant Gajendra, held in a lotus pond by a nāga and makara, raising a lotus in his trunk as Viṣṇu arrives on Garuḍa to free him. It is one of the earliest monumental depictions of the Gajendramokṣa story.
details: The temple was found in jungle growth c. 1871 by Charles Strahan, visited by Cunningham in 1875, surveyed by P. C. Mukerji in 1899, and published by M. S. Vats (1952). The three great wall niches face north (Gajendramokṣa), east (Nara-Nārāyaṇa) and south (Anantaśayana).

summary: The south wall niche of the Daśāvatāra temple at Deogarh shows Viṣṇu reclining on the seven-hooded serpent Śeṣa (Ananta), with Lakṣmī at his feet and a small four-headed Brahmā above. name: Rāmāyaṇa and Kṛṣṇa plinth panels, Deogarh
summary: A series of relief panels from the plinth of the Daśāvatāra temple at Deogarh, many now in the National Museum, New Delhi. Rāmāyaṇa scenes include Ahalyā's release, the departure into exile, Atri's hermitage, Śūrpaṇakhā, Sītā's abduction, Sugrīva's victory and Hanumān bringing the mountain of herbs. Kṛṣṇa scenes include the birth in prison, Nanda and Yaśodā with Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, the fight with Kaṃsa and the theft of the bathers' clothes. They are among the earliest narrative cycles of both epics in stone.
details: Daya Ram Sahni found Rāmāyaṇa panels buried near the foundation in 1918. The main body of loose sculpture is in the National Museum, New Delhi, with a few pieces in the ASI site museum at Deogarh. Accession numbers were not verified. The National Museum also has a Deogarh relief of Devakī handing the newborn Kṛṣṇa to Vasudeva. Other panels show Vāmana and Trivikrama and Narasiṃha saving Prahlāda.

name: Rāmāyaṇa panels, Nachna
summary: Stone relief panels at the Gupta-period temples of Nachna (Nachna-Kuthara), Madhya Pradesh, show episodes of the Rāmāyaṇa. They include Rāvaṇa disguised as a mendicant asking Sītā for alms, Sītā rebuking Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma hesitating to shoot Vālin, and the monkey leaders including Hanumān paying respect to Rāma. They are counted among the earliest known Rāmāyaṇa friezes, though older single Rāmāyaṇa-related scenes are claimed at Bharhut and Sanchi.
details: Cunningham published the site in 1885 (ASI Reports vol. 21). Joanna Williams (1982) analyses the Pārvatī temple and its sculpture. Michael Meister dates the Pārvatī temple to c. 465 CE and George Michell a few decades later. Two rock inscriptions attributed to Vyāghradeva (c. 470–490 CE) attest the region's importance. This record could not verify whether the panels are in situ or in a museum.

dates.label: second half of the 5th century CE

location.label: Nachna, Panna district, Madhya Pradesh, India

attributes.findspot: Nachna temple site (Pārvatī temple area)

limits: Shows that Araṇya- and Kiṣkindhā-kāṇḍa episodes were sculpted in central India by c. 500 CE. It does not date the composition of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa and is not evidence for the historicity of its events.
openQuestions: Where are the Nachna Rāmāyaṇa panels now held (in situ, Allahabad Museum or elsewhere)?

name: Gold archer-type coin of Candragupta II with Śrī (Cleveland 1977.62)
summary: A gold coin (dīnāra) of Candragupta II, c. 400 CE, in the Cleveland Museum of Art (accession 1977.62). The obverse shows the king as an archer with bow and arrow. The reverse shows Śrī, the goddess of good fortune (Lakṣmī), seated on a lotus. The archer type is the commonest Gupta gold coinage.
details: The museum dates the coin to c. 400 CE and Candragupta II's reign to c. 380–415 CE. The seated goddess on Gupta reverses is generally taken as Lakṣmī/Śrī, and her type is often derived from the Kuṣāṇa goddess Ardochsho. That derivation is a scholarly argument and is not stated in the museum record.

dates.label: c. 400 CE (reign of Candragupta II, c. 380–415)

attributes.iconography: obverse king as archer; reverse Śrī seated on a lotus

limits: Shows Śrī-Lakṣmī as a royal emblem of fortune on Gupta coinage c. 400 CE. It does not show the narrative of Lakṣmī's emergence from the churning of the ocean.

name: Kārttikeya (peacock) type gold coins of Kumāragupta I
summary: A gold coin type of the Gupta king Kumāragupta I (c. 415–455 CE). The obverse shows the king feeding a peacock, with the legend Śrī-Mahendra Kumāraḥ. The reverse shows the god Kārttikeya (Kumāra, Skanda) seated on his peacock. The king's name, Kumāra, puns on the god's.
details: This is a coin type, not a single specimen. No museum specimen with a verified accession number is recorded here.

attributes.iconography: obverse king feeding peacock; reverse Kārttikeya seated on peacock

limits: Shows royal veneration of Skanda-Kārttikeya in the 5th century CE. It does not show the textual birth narrative of Skanda, and the obverse legend reading is taken from a secondary source.
openQuestions: Which museum specimen (with accession) best represents the type?

name: Kṛṣṇa Govardhanadhara from Varanasi (Bharat Kala Bhavan)
summary: A Gupta-period stone sculpture of Kṛṣṇa lifting Mount Govardhana, recovered from Varanasi and held in the Bharat Kala Bhavan museum, Banaras Hindu University. It is dated to the 4th–6th century CE, with some records giving the 5th century. It is one of the earliest monumental images of the Govardhana episode.
details: The Commons record and the Krishna article date it to the Gupta period, 4th–6th century CE. An ANU archive photograph record labels it 'Krishna Giridara, 5th cent. A.D. Bharat Kala Bhavan, Benares'. No accession number was verified.

attributes.findspot: Varanasi
attributes.repository: Bharat Kala Bhavan, Banaras Hindu University, Varanasi

limits: Shows that the cowherd (Gopāla) cycle of Kṛṣṇa, as narrated in the Harivaṃśa and Purāṇas, was represented in Gupta-period sculpture. It does not date those texts precisely.
openQuestions: What is the Bharat Kala Bhavan accession number for this sculpture?

name: Gangdhar stone inscription of the time of Viśvavarman (423/424 CE)
aliases: Gangdhar stela of the time of Visvavarman
summary: A Sanskrit stone inscription from Gangdhar (Jhalawar district, Rajasthan), dated year 480 of the Mālava (Kṛta) era, the 13th of the bright half of Kārttika (423/424 CE), in the reign of the Aulikara king Viśvavarman. It records that his minister Mayūrākṣaka built a temple of Viṣṇu, a “terrifying abode of the divine Mothers” (Mātṛkās), and a well.
details: Fleet edited it in 1888 and Sircar later re-edited it. The description of the Mothers' shrine has been read as the earliest description of a Tantric temple. Michael Willis re-edited the key verse and noted the word is tāntra, not tantra, which bears on that reading.

location.label: Gangdhar, Jhalawar district, Rajasthan, India (findspot)

attributes.findspot: Gangdhar, on the Kali Sindh river
attributes.reading: minister Mayūrākṣaka built a temple of Viṣṇu, an abode of the divine Mothers, and a well (summary per Wikipedia translation)

limits: Establishes that a Viṣṇu temple and a shrine of the Mothers were founded together in western Mālwa in 423/424 CE. The inference that the Mothers' cult was Tantric depends on contested readings.
openQuestions: Where is the Gangdhar stone now held?

name: Mandasor inscription of the silk-weavers' guild (Mālava years 493 and 529)
aliases: Mandsaur stone inscription of Kumaragupta and Bandhuvarman
summary: A Sanskrit verse inscription from Mandasor (ancient Daśapura), composed by Vatsabhaṭṭi. It records that a guild of silk weavers who had migrated from Lāṭa (south Gujarat) built a temple of the Sun in Mālava year 493 (436/437 CE), while Kumāragupta ruled the earth and Bandhuvarman was lord of Daśapura. It also records that the same guild repaired the temple in year 529 (472/473 CE).
details: Vatsabhaṭṭi composed the praśasti in ornate kāvya verse, and its literary quality is often compared with Kālidāsa. Scholars disagree over whether the Kumāragupta of the inscription is Kumāragupta I (the majority view) or Kumāragupta II (R. C. Majumdar). The year conversions follow the Mālava/Vikrama era.

location.label: Mandsaur (ancient Daśapura), Madhya Pradesh, India (findspot area)

attributes.findspot: Mandasor (Daśapura)

limits: Shows a craft guild patronising Sun worship in Mālwa in the 5th century, and the date of a lost temple's construction and repair. The temple structure itself is not identified with any surviving building here.
openQuestions: Where is the stone now kept, and is any trace of the Sun temple identifiable?

name: Dadhimatī Mātā inscription of Dhruhlaṇa (Gupta year 289 = 608 CE)
summary: A Sanskrit inscription found in the ancient temple of the goddess Dadhimatī between Goth and Mānglod (Nagaur district, Rajasthan). It is dated Gupta year 289, 13th of the dark half of Śrāvaṇa (608 CE). Its lines 11–12 contain a verse that the editor identified as a quotation from the Devī Māhātmya, beginning sarva-maṅgala-māṅgalye. This gives a firm terminus ante quem for that text.
details: Pandit Ram Karna published the slab in Epigraphia Indica vol. XI, no. 31. It had been found upside down in a corner of the temple hall. The text is prose except lines 11–12, which give the verse. According to the commentary reported on Jatland, the editor located it in Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa ch. 91, v. 9, in the edition he used; that is the Nārāyaṇī hymn of the Devī Māhātmya, whose chapter numbering differs between editions. The Devī Māhātmya article on Wikipedia cites the inscription as evidence that the text existed before the 7th century.

dates.label: Gupta year 289 = 608 CE
dates.basis: dated in the Gupta era (= Vikrama 665)

location.label: Dadhimatī Mātā temple, between Goth and Mānglod, Nagaur district, Rajasthan, India (findspot)

attributes.findspot: temple of Dadhimatī, Goth–Mānglod boundary (found lying in the temple hall)
attributes.reading: verse in lines 11–12 beginning “sarva-maṅgala-māṅgalye” (Devī Māhātmya), per the EI edition

limits: Fixes a date by which at least one Devī Māhātmya verse circulated (608 CE). It does not show that the whole text existed in its present form, and it does not date the narratives of the Goddess's battles.
openQuestions: Which verse number does the quotation correspond to in the critical numbering of the Devī Māhātmya (ch. 11 in common editions)?

name: Eighteen-armed dancing Śiva, Bādāmi Cave 1
summary: A rock-cut relief about 1.5 m high, to the right of the entrance of Bādāmi Cave 1, showing Śiva dancing with eighteen arms. Some hands hold a drum, a flame, a serpent, a trident and an axe, and Gaṇeśa and Nandi are beside him. It belongs to the late 6th-century Cālukya cave series and is one of the earliest monumental images of the dancing Śiva.
details: Alice Boner read the arrangement of the arms as a geometric division of time, a cosmic wheel. Cave 1 itself is undated. The series is anchored by the Cave 3 inscription of 578 CE, and the cave numbers do not reflect the order of excavation.

dates.label: second half of the 6th century CE
dates.basis: style; relative to the dated Cave 3 (578 CE)

location.label: Bādāmi cave temples, Bagalkot district, Karnataka, India (in situ)

attributes.findspot: Bādāmi Cave 1, rock face right of entrance

limits: Shows the dancing Śiva as a monumental theme in 6th-century Karnataka. It is not the Cōḻa ānanda-tāṇḍava Naṭarāja form, and it does not date the Cidambaram tradition.

name: Bādāmi Cave 3 inscription of Maṅgaleśa (Śaka 500 = 578 CE)
summary: An inscription in Cave 3 at Bādāmi, dated Kārttika full moon of Śaka 500 (31 October or 1 November 578 CE) in the reign of the Cālukya king Kīrtivarman I. It records that his younger brother Maṅgaleśa made the Viṣṇu cave temple, called Mahāviṣṇugṛha or Lañjīśvara, “well-proportioned and of wonderful workmanship”, and gave land to the temple's garland-makers. It is the only dated cave at Bādāmi.
details: The pages checked describe the script as early (Old) Kannada. The Badami article calls it a Kannada-language record, but standard epigraphic literature treats the dedicatory text as Sanskrit in Kannada script. The language is therefore unresolved here. The Mangalesha article gives the date as 31 October 578 CE, and Michell (2017, cited on Wikipedia) gives 1 November 578.

location.label: Bādāmi cave temples, Bagalkot district, Karnataka, India (in situ)

attributes.findspot: Bādāmi Cave 3
attributes.language: unresolved (Sanskrit with early Kannada script per most editions; Wikipedia says Kannada)

limits: Dates the excavation of Cave 3 and shows royal Vaiṣṇava patronage by the Cālukyas in 578 CE. It does not date the other caves directly.
openQuestions: Confirm the language of the Cave 3 dedicatory inscription (Sanskrit vs Kannada) from Fleet's edition in Indian Antiquary.

name: Sadāśiva / Maheśamūrti (“Trimūrti”), Elephanta Cave 1
summary: A colossal three-headed bust, about 6–7 m high, carved on the south wall of the main cave at Elephanta near Mumbai. It shows Śiva with three faces: a fierce moustached face (Aghora-Bhairava), a calm central face (Tatpuruṣa) and a gentle face holding a lotus (Vāmadeva/Umā). Older literature called it a Trimūrti of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva; most modern scholars read it as Sadāśiva or Maheśamūrti. It dates to about the 6th century CE.
details: Heights given in the sources vary: 7 m, 6.27 m and 5.45 m. Contemporary scholars attribute the Great Cave to the Kalachuri king Kṛṣṇarāja and its completion to the second quarter of the 6th century, using coins, inscriptions, style and comparison with Ajanta. Older proposals range from the 5th to the 9th century, and the Rāṣṭrakūṭa attribution is now discredited. The caves were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987 (no. 244). They suffered damage in the Portuguese period.

dates.label: c. 525–575 CE (completion in the second quarter of the 6th century)

location.label: Elephanta Island (Gharapuri), Mumbai harbour, Maharashtra, India (in situ)

attributes.findspot: south wall of Cave 1 (Great Cave), facing the north entrance

limits: Shows a sophisticated multi-faced Śiva theology in western India by the 6th century. Reading the faces as specific Āgamic aspects is interpretive, and the image does not establish a Brahmā–Viṣṇu–Śiva 'trinity' doctrine.

name: Mahiṣāsuramardinī relief, Mamallapuram
summary: A large relief on the north wall of the rock-cut Mahiṣāsuramardinī maṇḍapa at Mamallapuram (Pallava, 7th century). It shows the eight-armed goddess Durgā riding a lion into battle against the buffalo-headed Mahiṣāsura, with attendants, one of whom holds a parasol over her. The opposite wall shows Viṣṇu reclining on Ādiśeṣa, with the demons Madhu and Kaiṭabha. It is considered one of the finest Pallava sculptures.
details: The goddess holds a sword, bow, arrows and bell in her right hands and a noose, conch and dagger in her left, and drives Mahiṣa back with arrows. The cave is dated to the mid or late 7th century, under Narasiṃhavarman I Māmalla (630–668) and his successors. The maṇḍapa's interior is 9.8 × 4.6 × 3.8 m.

location.label: Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram), Chengalpattu district, Tamil Nadu, India (in situ)

attributes.findspot: Mahiṣāsuramardinī maṇḍapa, north wall

limits: Shows which myths a 7th-century Pallava court chose to monumentalise. It does not date the texts narrating them or establish the events.

name: Great relief of Mamallapuram (“Arjuna's Penance” / “Descent of the Gaṅgā”)
summary: An open-air relief about 29 × 13 m carved across two granite boulders at Mamallapuram (Pallava, 7th century). A natural cleft between them, filled with nāgas, may once have carried water. Gods, celestials, sages, hunters and animals converge on the cleft. A figure standing on one leg in austerity before Śiva is read either as Arjuna seeking the Pāśupata weapon (the Kirātārjunīya episode) or as Bhagīratha bringing the Gaṅgā to earth. Which reading is right is debated (claim:mamallapuram-relief-identity).
details: Wikipedia links the relief to Narasiṃhavarman I (630–668), son of Mahendravarman I, and to his victory over Pulakeśin II. A famous detail shows a cat standing on one leg in mock austerity among mice, which Wikipedia relates to a fable. Padma Kaimal (1994) argues the relief is deliberately ambiguous and supports both readings.

dates.label: 7th century CE (reign of Narasiṃhavarman I, 630–668, as attributed)
7th – early 8th century CE
dates.basis: range of Pallava attributions in the literature

location.label: Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram), Tamil Nadu, India (in situ)

attributes.findspot: open-air rock face, Mamallapuram

limits: Shows which myths a 7th-century Pallava court chose to monumentalise. It does not date the texts narrating them or establish the events. The identity of the central narrative is disputed.

name: The Mamallapuram great relief depicts the Descent of the Gaṅgā (not Arjuna's penance)
summary: Scholars disagree over whether the central ascetic of the great relief at Mamallapuram is Bhagīratha, whose penance brought the Gaṅgā to earth, or Arjuna performing austerities to obtain the Pāśupata weapon from Śiva. Some argue the ambiguity is intentional. This claim records the Descent-of-the-Gaṅgā reading and the evidence for and against it.
details:
For the Gaṅgā reading: the central cleft is lined with nāgas and nāginīs in water, and was perhaps fed with water from above, so the whole composition converges on a descending river. Śiva's boon-granting gesture also fits Bhagīratha's story.

For the Arjuna reading: the emaciated ascetic stands on one leg before Śiva, who carries a weapon, the Pāśupata, and the hunters and boar may evoke the Kirātārjunīya. Bhāravi's Kirātārjunīya was well known in the Pallava south. Kaimal (1994) argues the relief is a deliberate double reading that served Pallava royal ideology.
limits: Either identification describes 7th-century Pallava iconography only; neither bears on the historicity of Bhagīratha or Arjuna.

name: Rāvaṇa shaking Mount Kailāsa (Rāvaṇānugraha), Kailāsa temple, Ellora
summary: A deep-cut relief at the monolithic Kailāsa temple (Ellora Cave 16). It shows the ten-headed Rāvaṇa trapped beneath Mount Kailāsa, trying to shake it, while Śiva and Pārvatī sit above and Śiva steadies the mountain with his foot. It is often described as one of the finest pieces of Indian sculpture. It dates to the 8th century under the Rāṣṭrakūṭas, or a few decades later according to some authors.
details: The temple has no dedicatory inscription. Its attribution to the Rāṣṭrakūṭa Kṛṣṇa I (c. 756–773) rests on the Vadodara copper plates of Karkarāja II (c. 812–813) and the Kadaba grant of Govinda Prabhūtavarṣa, which praise a Kṛṣṇarāja as builder. Dhavalikar dates the Rāvaṇa panel about three or four decades after the main shrine, and Goetz assigned it to the reign of Kṛṣṇa III.

dates.basis: attribution of the temple to Kṛṣṇa I (c. 756–773) via later copper plates; style
dates.view: Dhavalikar (3–4 decades after the main shrine)

dates.label: mid-10th century CE (reign of Kṛṣṇa III)

location.label: Kailāsa temple, Ellora, Aurangabad district, Maharashtra, India (in situ)

attributes.findspot: Kailāsa temple complex (Cave 16)

limits: Shows the Rāvaṇānugraha myth as a Rāṣṭrakūṭa-era Śaiva theme. It is evidence of 8th–10th-century narrative and cult, not of the event itself.

name: Aihole inscription of Pulakeśin II (Ravikīrti)
summary: A 19-line Sanskrit verse praśasti on the Meguti Jain temple at Aihole, composed by the Jain poet Ravikīrti for the Cālukya king Pulakeśin II. It is dated both Śaka 556 and 3735 years after the Bhārata war, equivalent to 634/635 CE. Ravikīrti claims to have reached the fame of Kālidāsa and Bhāravi, which makes the inscription a terminus ante quem for both poets. It also gives the Cālukya account of Pulakeśin's defeat of Harṣa.
details:
Verses 33–34 give the two dates. Fleet read the Bhārata-war reckoning correctly in 1879, after an earlier error. Lines 18–19 are later additions in a different style. The stone is set in the wall between the maṇḍapa and the garbhagṛha of the Meguti temple. Fleet published a photolithograph in 1876 and a revised text in 1879, and F. Kielhorn a revised text and translation in Epigraphia Indica vol. VI (1900–01).

The Bhārata-war era: 3735 years before 634/635 CE gives c. 3102/3101 BCE, the conventional Kali-yuga epoch. The inscription shows that this traditional chronology was in use in 7th-century Karnataka. It is not independent evidence for the date of the war. The claim that Pulakeśin defeated Harṣa is contested by Xuanzang's account.

name: Changu Narayan pillar inscription of Mānadeva
summary: A Sanskrit inscription on a stone pillar at the Changu Narayan temple near Bhaktapur (Kathmandu Valley), issued by the Licchavi king Mānadeva. It is dated Saṃvat 386, conventionally equated with 464 CE, and is often called the earliest dated inscription of Nepal. It was first published by Bhagvanlal Indraji and Georg Bühler (1885) and later by Sylvain Lévi.
details: The Wikipedia articles checked call it “one of the oldest pillar inscriptions in Nepal”, and the Mānadeva article calls it the earliest inscription of the Licchavi period. Secondary sources report a fragmentary Paśupati-area inscription of Saṃvat 381 that may be older, and some read Saṃvat 386 in another era as 495/96 CE. Both the 'earliest' label and the CE equivalent therefore remain disputed. Siddham catalogues the pillar's inscribed shafts separately. The present temple was rebuilt after damage, most recently after the 2015 earthquake.

name: Śivagṛha inscription (856 CE)
summary: An Old Javanese inscription on andesite, dated Śaka 778 (856 CE) by the chronogram wwalung gunung sang wiku. It was issued by Dyah Lokapāla (Rakai Kayuwangi) after the abdication of Rakai Pikatan (Jatiningrat). It describes the consecration of a great Śiva temple compound called Śivagṛha and the diversion of a river along its wall. J. G. de Casparis identified the compound with Prambanan (Candi Loro Jonggrang). The stone is in the National Museum of Indonesia, Jakarta (D.28).
details: The river diversion is usually identified with the Opak river, whose course was moved to run along the outer wall of the compound, freeing space for rows of subsidiary (perwara) shrines. The language (Old Javanese) and script (Kawi) follow de Casparis's edition and standard descriptions; the Wikipedia page checked gives only the translation.

dates.label: Śaka 778 = 856 CE
dates.basis: dated by chronogram in the Śaka era

attributes.findspot: Prambanan area, Central Java / Yogyakarta, Indonesia

limits: Dates the consecration of a Śiva temple compound in Central Java to 856 CE. Its identification with Prambanan is scholarly. It does not date the Rāmāyaṇa reliefs of Prambanan individually.

name: Chola bronze Naṭarāja (Cleveland Museum of Art 1930.331)
summary: A Cōḻa-period bronze of Śiva as Naṭarāja, lord of the dance, from Tamil Nadu, dated to the 11th century. It is 113 cm high and is in the Cleveland Museum of Art (accession 1930.331), bought in 1930 from the dealer C. T. Loo. It represents the classic ānanda-tāṇḍava form: Śiva dancing within a ring of flames on the dwarf of ignorance (Apasmāra), holding the drum and the flame.
details: The museum's record gives the title 'Nataraja, Shiva as the Lord of Dance', date 1000s, culture South India, Tamil Nadu, Chola period (900–1200s), medium bronze, overall 113 × 102 × 30 cm, base 35 × 24 cm, and credit line Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund. The provenance runs from C. T. Loo (1880–1957), New York, to the museum in 1930. The original temple is not recorded. Bronzes of this kind were carried in procession on poles passed through rings in the base. The Naṭarāja form is linked in Tamil Śaiva tradition with Cidambaram.

attributes.repository: Cleveland Museum of Art, Ohio, USA
attributes.provenance: C. T. Loo, New York → Cleveland Museum of Art (1930)
attributes.creditLine: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund

name: Shiva Nataraja, Rijksmuseum (AK-MAK-187)
summary: A Cōḻa bronze Naṭarāja from Tamil Nadu, dated c. 1100–1200, about 153 cm high, displayed at the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, as object AK-MAK-187. It is on loan from the Royal Asian Art Society in the Netherlands, which bought it from C. T. Loo, Paris, in 1935 with support from the Vereniging Rembrandt.
details: The museum record describes Śiva in the ānanda-tāṇḍava pose within a ring of fire, with the dwarf of ignorance beneath his foot, and notes that such bronzes were carried in processions using poles passed through the rings on the base. Dimensions are given as h 153 × w 114.5 cm. The record also lists other measurements and weights (40 kg and 255 kg), which presumably refer to the base or a mount.
